en: The Mātaṅga Chapter of the Jātaka,
Twenty-Verse Collection (Vīsatinipāta)
1. The Mātaṅga Jātaka:
“From where do you come, you who dress in rags, looking like a beggar covered in dust?”
“Why do you wear a rag from a rubbish heap around your neck?
Who are you, you who are unworthy of offerings?
“This food has been prepared for you, O illustrious one.”
They chew it, they eat it, and they drink it;
you know me as one who lives on what is given by others,
receiving the alms-food of those who stand up to give.
“This food has been prepared by me for the brahmins;
it is mine, given out of faith for my own sake.
Go away from here! Why do you stand here?”
“People like me do not give to you, O low-born one.
“They sow seed both on dry land and in the lowlands,
hoping for fruit in the fertile field.”
"With this faith, give a gift;
perhaps you might thus satisfy those worthy of offerings.
"The fields in this world are known to me."
Those for whom I plant seeds—
those brahmins who are endowed with noble birth—
are here the most excellent fields.”
“Pride of birth and excessive conceit,
greed, hatred, intoxication, and delusion—
those in whom all these unwholesome qualities exist,”
These are indeed unwholesome fields here:
pride in birth, excessive arrogance,
greed, hatred, intoxication, and delusion.
“Those in whom all these faults do not exist—
those here are truly excellent fields.
“Where have the torch-bearers gone?”
Whether it be the preceptor or Gaṇḍakucchi,
having inflicted upon him both punishment and beating,
seize this wretch by the neck and drive him away!
“You dig at a mountain with your claws,
you chew iron with your teeth;
you strike against fire.”
“You who revile the seer.
Having said this, Mātaṅga,
the seer who was devoted to truth, [spoke].
He departed into the sky while the brahmins looked on.
With his head turned back and twisted around, he said:
He stretches out his arm, though it is no longer functional;
his eyes are white like those of a dead man.
Who has brought my son to such a state?
“Here has come the ascetic Dummavāsī,
ragged like a dust-demon;
he wears a rag from the rubbish heap around his neck.”
"Thus you have made this son of yours in such a way.
"To which direction has he gone, O youth of vast wisdom?
Explain this matter to me, young men."
"Having gone, let us confess our transgression;
perhaps we may yet obtain our son's life.
"The one of vast wisdom departed through the air,"
Like the moon on the fifteenth day of the waxing fortnight,
that seer of noble character, true to his promise, proceeded toward the eastern direction.
“With his head turned back,
he stretches out his arm, useless for action;
his eyes are white like those of a dead man.”
"Who has made my son thus?
"There are indeed powerful yakkhas who have followed after these sages of noble form."
"Having perceived that my mind was corrupted and agitated,
the yakkhas indeed made my son thus:
'The yakkhas have made my son thus.'"
Do not be angry with me, O celibate one;
it is to you alone that I have gone for refuge at your feet,
O monk, having been overcome by grief for my son.
“Indeed, even now there is no corruption of mind whatsoever in me;
but your son is intoxicated by the pride of Vedic knowledge.”
“He does not know the meaning, having learned the Vedas by chance.
“Surely, O Bhikkhu, in a mere moment,
a person’s perception becomes utterly deluded.”
"Forgive this one offense, O one of vast wisdom;
the wise do not become slaves to anger.
"And here is my alms-food from what has been set aside..."
"Let Maṇḍabya eat, for he is of little wisdom;
let the yakkhas not harm him,
and he shall become your son, free from disease."
“Maṇḍavya, you are a fool of limited wisdom,
you who are unskilled regarding fields of merit;
you give gifts to those with great afflictions.”
When defiled actions are unrestrained,
matted hair, long locks, and antelope skins are worn,
yet the mouth is overgrown like a mossy well.
Behold this wretched-looking assembly;
neither matted hair nor deerskin protects one who lacks wisdom.
For those in whom passion and hatred [still remain]...
And ignorance has been faded away;
for those Arhats whose taints are destroyed,
what is given to them bears great fruit.
The Mātaṅga Jātaka is first.
